title: Holderness: Hard vs Soft Engineering
welcome_lead: Stand on Europe's fastest-eroding coast and weigh the politics of defending it.
meta_desc: A-Level Geography Coastal Landscapes: Holderness case, hard engineering, managed realignment.
final_note: You have evaluated the costs of trying to hold back the sea.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Holderness coast (61 km from Flamborough Head to Spurn Point) retreats at an average ~1.8 m/yr, locally up to 10 m/yr. Since Roman times ~29 villages have been lost (Ravenser Odd, Kilnsea). The cliffs are unconsolidated boulder clay deposited by Devensian ice, easily eroded by hydraulic action and slumping after rainfall saturates the clay. Sediment fed south by longshore drift built Spurn Spit (5.5 km long).

At Hornsea, sea walls (~£2m/km), rock revetments and groynes protect the town. At Mappleton, two rock groynes and a revetment built in 1991 (£2m) saved 50 homes and the B1242 road. However, by terminal groyne syndrome, downdrift erosion accelerated to ~4 m/yr at Cowden, where the MoD Cowden firing range and Great Cowden farmhouse have been lost. This illustrates how interventions externalise costs along the cell.

Soft engineering options include beach nourishment (e.g. Mablethorpe, Lincolnshire), dune stabilisation (marram grass planting), and managed realignment at sites like Medmerry (Sussex, 2013) where embankments were breached to recreate 183 ha of intertidal habitat, providing flood protection and biodiversity. Shoreline Management Plans for Holderness now designate stretches as no active intervention due to unfavourable cost-benefit ratios.

mcqs.q: Why might managed retreat be more sustainable than building a sea wall?
options: Managed retreat means letting all coastal towns disappear into the sea.
Sea walls always solve coastal erosion problems permanently.
Soft engineering means using softer materials like sand instead of concrete.
Sea walls are expensive, deflect erosion elsewhere and reflect wave energy worsening beach loss; managed retreat works with natural processes, creates habitat and is cheaper long-term.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between hard and soft engineering for flood management?
options: Hard engineering always works better than soft engineering at preventing floods.
Hard engineering uses built structures (dams, levees, channelisation) to control flow; soft engineering works with natural processes (afforestation, wetland restoration, floodplain zoning).
It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.
Soft engineering means using softer materials like sand instead of concrete.

mcqs.q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.
The greenhouse effect is entirely man-made and harmful.
Managed retreat means letting all coastal towns disappear into the sea.
The strengthening of the natural greenhouse effect by human activities (mainly burning fossil fuels) which add CO2 and other gases to the atmosphere.
